$comment: The rate pages: what Roblox pays, which rate applies to which part of a balance, what changed in September 2025, and the two conversion directions people confuse. Nothing here may be shortened — 'Roblox decides which rate applies' is the sentence that stops a reader thinking the rate is a choice.

devexRates.threeRatesDescription: All three come from the same official Roblox documentation, checked on the date shown above.

whichApplies.p2: The split calculator models a mixed balance

timeline.p1: Standard rate increased to 0.0038 USD per Earned Robux
timeline.p2: Roblox states this as 114 USD for 30,000 Earned Robux, up from 105. Balances earned before this moment continue to convert at the previous rate and are cashed out first.
timeline.p3: Standard rate of 0.0035 USD per Earned Robux
timeline.p4: 105 USD for 30,000 Earned Robux. Still applied to the portion of any balance earned before the transition.

comparison.p1: The increase is about 8.6% across the board, since it is a change to a single multiplier.

legacyBalances.p1: The split calculator lets you model a mixed balance
legacyBalances.p2: if you know roughly how yours divides, but treat the result as an estimate built on your own assumption about the split.

noForecast.p1: Roblox has changed the rate before and may change it again. Nobody outside Roblox knows whether or when, and a prediction dressed up as analysis would be a guess with a confident tone. This page records only changes that official documentation confirms, each with its effective date. When a change happens it appears here and in the

prose.legacySplit: Roblox cashes out the pre-transition portion of a balance at 0.0035 first, then the rest at 0.0038. The split is Roblox’s own accounting of when each Robux was earned — it is not something a creator selects or can adjust.
prose.whenItChanges: Roblox has changed the rate before and may change it again. Nobody outside Roblox knows whether or when, and a prediction dressed up as analysis would be a guess with a confident tone. This page records only changes that official documentation confirms, each with its effective date. When a change happens it appears here and in the {changelog}, along with the date it was verified.

requirements.intro: What Roblox actually requires before a DevEx request can be submitted, taken from its own documentation rather than from repeated third-party summaries.
requirements.minimumDescription: The number everybody looks up first, and the one most often quoted out of date.
requirements.minimumDiagramCaption: Not drawn to scale: there is no upper limit on a balance, so any width for the eligible side would be invented. The break is the only part that carries meaning.
requirements.notApprovalHeading: Meeting the threshold is not approval
requirements.notApprovalDescription: This distinction is the single most important thing on this page.
requirements.checklistDescription: Getting these in place before you apply avoids the obvious delays. Tick them off as you go — these steps are usually done days apart, and progress is kept in your own browser.
requirements.misunderstandingsDescription: Each of these is something creators repeat to each other, alongside what the documentation actually says.

items.earnedOnly: Earned Robux specifically — a balance made up of purchased Robux does not qualify however large it is.
items.minimumAgeDetail: Roblox documents 13 as the minimum age to participate in the programme.
items.verifiedEmailDetail: The address on the account must be verified before a request can proceed.
items.portalAccountDetail: Requests are submitted through the official DevEx portal, not through the site.
items.taxFormDetail: An IRS form W-9 for United States taxpayers, or a W-8 for non-United States taxpayers.
items.complianceDetail: The account must comply with the Roblox Terms of Use and Community Standards.

requirements.checkBalanceLink: Check your balance against the minimum

checklist.verifyEmail: Verify the email address on your Roblox account.
checklist.portalAccount: Create and confirm access to your DevEx portal account.

minimum.p1: {minimumEarnedRobux} Earned Robux is the threshold to submit a request. At the current standard rate that balance is worth about
minimum.p2: before any payment-provider fees or tax.

notApproval.p1: No calculator, including this one, can tell you whether a DevEx request will be approved. Roblox decides which of your Robux count as Earned Robux and whether your account and request meet its criteria. Anyone telling you otherwise — including any site promising a guaranteed payout — is not in a position to know.

checklist.p1: Confirm your balance is genuinely Earned Robux and has reached {minimumEarnedRobux}.
checklist.p2: Complete the correct tax form — W-9 if you are a United States taxpayer, W-8 otherwise.
checklist.p3: Check your account is in good standing against the Terms of Use and Community Standards.
checklist.p4: Decide where the money is going, and check what your bank or payment provider will charge to receive it.

minimum10k.reality: It is 30,000 Earned Robux. The lower figure circulates on third-party sites that have not been updated, and it is not what current Roblox documentation says.

anyBalance.claim: Any Robux balance counts toward the minimum.
anyBalance.reality: Only Earned Robux count. A balance made up of purchased Robux does not qualify however large it is.

reaching30k.claim: Reaching 30,000 means you will be paid.
reaching30k.reality: It means you can submit a request. Roblox reviews each one and decides which Robux qualify as earned.

age18.claim: You need to be 18 to use DevEx.
age18.reality: Roblox documents a minimum age of 13. The separate 18+ condition concerns the age verification of the players who spent the Robux, and affects the rate rather than your eligibility.

threshold.below: Below the line, a DevEx request cannot be submitted at all. Being close to it counts for nothing, and the shortfall has to be earned — it cannot be bought.
threshold.above: At or above the line, a request can be submitted. It is then reviewed, and meeting the threshold is not the same as being approved.

prose.earnedOnly: The word that matters is {earned}. Robux you bought do not count toward it, and neither does gift card credit. {earnedRobuxLink}

earnedRobux.intro: The distinction that decides whether a DevEx payout is possible at all — and the one most often missed until a request is refused.
earnedRobux.sortingCaption: A summary of the sorting. The full lists, and what Roblox says about each route, are in the two sections below.
earnedRobux.balanceDiffersTitle: Why your balance and your Earned Robux differ
earnedRobux.countsDescription: These are the routes by which Robux normally become Earned Robux. Roblox makes the final determination for any specific balance.
earnedRobux.doesNotCountDescription: Robux acquired these ways sit in the same balance but are treated differently.
earnedRobux.pendingDescription: Newly earned Robux are not immediately available, which surprises creators watching a balance climb.
earnedRobux.groupFundsDescription: Robux held by a group are not the same as Robux held by you.
earnedRobux.staysButNeverQualifies: Stays in the balance, but never qualifies

definition.p1: The portion of your Robux balance that came from creator activity — other people spending Robux on something you made — rather than from Robux you acquired any other way. DevEx converts Earned Robux only. Your account shows a single Robux number, but Roblox tracks where each part of it came from, and that internal accounting is what determines eligibility.
definition.p2: — the balance DevEx converts, and the only balance that counts toward the {minimumEarnedRobux} minimum. Roblox makes the final determination for any specific balance.
definition.p4: If you have ever bought Robux, received them from a membership, or redeemed a gift card, part of your balance is not earned. That part cannot be cashed out, and it does not count toward the 30,000 minimum either.

qualifying.p1: In each case Roblox has already taken its platform commission before the Robux reach you — creators receive 70% of what a player spends on an in-experience purchase.
qualifying.p2: Work out what you keep on a sale

notQualifying.p1: The two are compared side by side here

pending.p1: Robux from a recent purchase typically spend a period as pending before becoming available, which protects against reversed transactions. Pending Robux are not yet part of the balance you can act on. Roblox documents the current holding behaviour in the Creator Hub, and because that behaviour has changed over time this page does not state a specific number of days — check the official documentation for the figure that applies now.

qualifying.developerProducts: Robux from players buying developer products inside an experience you own
qualifying.passes: Robux from pass purchases in your experience
qualifying.privateServers: Your share of private server subscriptions
qualifying.avatarItems: Your creator share of avatar items you made and sold
qualifying.experienceSubscriptions: Your share of experience subscriptions where these are available to you

notQualifying.purchased: Robux you bought yourself, in any package or at any price
notQualifying.giftCards: Robux from a gift card or promotional code
notQualifying.membership: Robux included with a Roblox membership as a monthly grant
notQualifying.trade: Robux received from another player in a trade
notQualifying.transferred: Robux transferred into your account from outside creator earnings

accepted.passesAndProducts: Players buying passes and developer products in your experience
accepted.subscriptions: Your share of private server and experience subscriptions
accepted.avatarItems: Your creator share of avatar items you made

rejected.purchased: Robux you bought yourself, at any price

prose.groupFunds: Earnings from an experience owned by a group accumulate in the group’s funds rather than in any individual account. DevEx operates on a personal account, so group funds have to reach a personal balance through a payout before they are relevant to a DevEx request. If you are splitting revenue with collaborators, agree how that works before the money arrives rather than after — and check the current official documentation for how group payouts are treated, since this is an area Roblox has changed before.
prose.retailUnrelated: This is also why the retail price of Robux and the DevEx rate are unrelated numbers. Buying Robux is a purchase; DevEx is Roblox paying a creator.

feesAndTaxes.intro: Three separate things sit between the DevEx conversion and the money reaching your account. None of them is the DevEx rate.
feesAndTaxes.notTaxAdviceTitle: This page is not tax advice
feesAndTaxes.threeDeductionsDescription: They apply in sequence, and confusing them is how creators end up with a number that is badly wrong.
feesAndTaxes.sequenceCaption: Each stage is a different party taking a different kind of cut, in this order. Roblox sets none of them, and this site publishes a figure for none of them.
feesAndTaxes.providerFeesDescription: The one deduction you can find out in advance, and probably should.
feesAndTaxes.conversionDescription: Why the figure on this site and the figure in your account differ.
feesAndTaxes.incomeTaxDescription: The part this site deliberately will not answer for you.
feesAndTaxes.modelDescription: Open the fee and tax controls below the currency selector and enter your own percentages.
feesAndTaxes.notMarketplaceHeading: Not to be confused with the marketplace fee
feesAndTaxes.notMarketplaceDescription: The 30% platform commission is a different thing at a different point in time.
feesAndTaxes.marketplaceDiagramCaption: The split happens when the player spends, long before DevEx is involved. Percentages come from the rate registry, not from this drawing.

diagram.balanceDevExConverts: This is the balance DevEx later converts.
diagram.takenOnceHere: Taken once, here — not again at cash-out.
diagram.devexPayoutNote: What the documented rate produces from your eligible Earned Robux. This is the figure the calculator estimates.
diagram.providerFeeNote: Often a percentage plus a fixed amount, charged for delivering the money.
diagram.conversionNote: Applied only if you are paid in something other than US dollars, at their rate plus a margin.
diagram.incomeTaxNote: A payout is income. What applies, and when, depends on your country and your circumstances.
diagram.whatReachesYouNote: Lower than the estimate above, by an amount only your own provider and tax position can tell you.
diagram.marketplaceTotal: 100 Robux spent by a player inside your experience

feesAndTaxes.ogImageAlt: Provider fees, then conversion, then income tax — none of them Roblox’s

intro.p1: Nothing here tells you what you owe. Tax depends on where you live, your circumstances and your total income, and this site has no way of knowing any of that. The estimator below uses whatever percentage you enter so you can model your own situation. For an actual answer, speak to a qualified adviser in your country.

threeLayers.p1: A DevEx payout is income. How much tax applies, and when, depends entirely on your country and your circumstances. Roblox requires a W-9 or W-8 precisely because this is taxable.

currency.p1: Local-currency estimates here use European Central Bank reference rates, published once each working day. They are a reference, not a quote: no bank trades at them. Your provider will apply its own rate, usually with a margin built in, so treat a converted figure here as an indication of scale rather than a prediction of what lands in your account.

tax.p1: There is no universal percentage, and publishing one would be actively harmful — a creator in one country could plan around a figure that is wrong for them by a factor of two. What this site does instead is let you enter your own estimate and see it applied to the real payout figure, so the arithmetic is done for you even though the rate is yours.
tax.p2: A practical note that is not advice: the tax is generally owed on the income, not on what is left after fees, and it is usually owed in the year the payout is received rather than the year the Robux were earned. Confirm both with someone qualified.

notTheMarketplaceFee.p1: Roblox takes 30% when a player spends Robux in your experience — you receive 70%, and that 70% is what becomes Earned Robux. DevEx then converts those Earned Robux. The commission is not applied a second time at cash-out, and any calculator that subtracts 30% from a DevEx payout is double-counting it.
notTheMarketplaceFee.p2: Work out the marketplace fee separately

prose.currencyMargin: The DevEx rate is stated in US dollars. If you are paid in another currency, someone converts it, and they apply their own rate plus a margin. That margin is why your bank’s figure will not match a reference rate.
prose.providerFeeTerm: Whatever service delivers the money may charge for doing so — often a percentage plus a fixed amount per payout. This is between you and that provider; Roblox does not set it and neither does this site.
prose.noFeeTable: Fee structures vary by provider, country and payout method, so this page does not publish a table of them — any figure would be out of date or wrong for most readers. Check what your own provider charges before you submit a request, then enter that figure in the calculator below to see it applied. On a small payout a fixed fee can be a noticeable share of the total; on a large one the percentage matters more.

robuxToUsd.intro: Two different questions hide behind the same search. This page answers both separately rather than blending them into one misleading number.
robuxToUsd.twoAnswersDescription: Asking what Robux are worth in dollars only has one answer once you say which direction the money is travelling.
robuxToUsd.noUniversalRateTitle: Why this site publishes no universal purchase rate
robuxToUsd.payoutVsPriceHeading: Creator payout compared with purchase price
robuxToUsd.payoutVsPriceDescription: The two numbers are different by design, and the gap is not a fee anyone is charging you.
robuxToUsd.differencesLabel: How creator payout and purchase price differ
robuxToUsd.differencesCaption: Differences between a DevEx creator payout and a Robux retail purchase
robuxToUsd.formulaDescription: One multiplication, stated openly so you can check it.
robuxToUsd.commonAmountsDescription: Calculated at all three documented rates. Amounts below the minimum are marked.

comparison.ratePayout: Documented and fixed at 0.0038 USD per eligible Earned Robux
comparison.ratePurchase: Varies by package, region, platform and promotion
comparison.reversiblePurchase: One way — purchased Robux cannot be sold back

twoAnswers.p2: You earned Robux from players spending in your experience, and you want to convert them to cash. That goes through DevEx at a documented rate, and it is what the calculator above estimates. It applies only to eligible Earned Robux, and only from 30,000 upward.
twoAnswers.p4: You want to know what a Robux package costs. Roblox sets that price by package, region, platform and any promotion running at the time. It is a retail price, not an exchange rate, and it moves independently of what DevEx pays.
twoAnswers.p5: There is no single number that is true for every package, country and platform, so quoting one would be inventing a figure. Check the current prices on
twoAnswers.p7: for what you would actually pay.

comparison.p1: The gap between the two exists because Roblox operates a platform, handles payment processing, and has already taken its 30% share at the point the Robux were spent.
comparison.p2: That earlier 30% is the marketplace fee

prose.officialPage: There is no single number that is true for every package, country and platform, so quoting one would be inventing a figure. Check {officialPage} for what you would actually pay.
prose.commissionOnce: The gap between the two exists because Roblox operates a platform, handles payment processing, and takes a commission for it. {marketplaceCalculator}, and it is not charged again at cash-out.

usdToRobux.intro: Set the payout you are aiming for and see exactly how many eligible Earned Robux it takes to get there.
usdToRobux.roundingDescription: Rounding down would leave you a fraction of a cent short of your own target, every time.
usdToRobux.minimumDescription: Arithmetic and eligibility are two different constraints, and the larger one wins.
usdToRobux.smallTargetTitle: A small target does not mean a small cash-out
usdToRobux.paceHeading: How long it takes at your pace
usdToRobux.paceDescription: The target tells you how much. This works out when — or, from a date, what you would have to earn to get there.
usdToRobux.commonTargetsDescription: Each row is computed with the same formula the calculator uses.
usdToRobux.commonTargetsLabel: Earned Robux required for common payout targets
usdToRobux.commonTargetsCaption: Eligible Earned Robux needed to reach common USD payout targets at the standard DevEx rate
usdToRobux.notBuyingHeading: This is not about buying Robux
usdToRobux.notBuyingDescription: The reverse direction has a very different answer depending on who is asking.
usdToRobux.ogImageAlt: Rounded up, because a partial Robux cannot be earned or exchanged

rounding.p1: A 1,000 dollar target divided by 0.0038 gives 263,157.89. Robux come in whole units, so 263,157 would pay {rate} — just under the target. Rounding up to 263,158 pays {rate2}, which clears it. That is why every figure on this page rounds up rather than to the nearest whole number.

minimum.p1: Roblox requires {minimumEarnedRobux} Earned Robux before a DevEx request can be submitted at all. If your target needs fewer than that, the minimum is what you actually have to reach — and it would pay {rate} rather than your original target.

planner.p1: A payout target is a distance. Turning it into a date needs one more fact — how fast you earn — and turning a date into a plan needs the same fact in reverse. Both are the same division:

buyingRobux.p1: This page answers the creator question: how much do I need to earn to receive a given amount of money. It does not tell you how many Robux a given amount of money will buy. Roblox prices Robux packages by region, platform and promotion, and there is no single rate that would be true for everyone — so this site does not publish one.
buyingRobux.p2: The distinction is explained in full on the Robux to USD page

prose.division: A payout target is a distance. Turning it into a date needs one more fact — how fast you earn — and turning a date into a plan needs the same fact in reverse. Both are the same division: {formula}, rounded up, because a part day earns nothing and a part Robux does not exist. Nothing here assumes your earnings grow, and nothing here is a date Roblox will pay on — Roblox publishes no DevEx processing time, so none is added.
prose.divisionFormula: days = remaining Earned Robux ÷ Earned Robux per day

robuxTax.intro: Work out what you keep after the Roblox platform commission, or what to charge to clear a target amount.
robuxTax.schemesDescription: Roblox uses different splits depending on what was sold and where it was bought.
robuxTax.schemesCaption: How Robux from a sale are divided, by sale type
robuxTax.progressiveDescription: For avatar items sold through the Marketplace, the creator share rises with the item’s price relative to its category price floor.
robuxTax.progressiveCaption: Creator revenue share by price as a multiple of the price floor
robuxTax.multipleTitle: Why the calculator asks for a multiple
robuxTax.scopeDescription: What this calculator does and does not cover.
robuxTax.notDevExHeading: This is not the DevEx rate
robuxTax.notDevExDescription: The two calculations happen at different times and must not be chained.

schemes.p5: Avatar item bought inside an experience
schemes.p6: Item creator and experience owner are paid separately
schemes.p7: If you sell your own item inside your own experience you receive both the creator share and the experience owner share, which comes to 70%.

notDevex.p1: The commission on this page applies at the moment a player spends Robux. What you keep becomes Earned Robux. DevEx then converts those Earned Robux to cash at its own rate, on a balance that has already had the commission taken. Subtracting 30% from a DevEx payout applies the same fee twice and understates what a creator receives.
notDevex.p2: Convert your Earned Robux to a payout estimate
notDevex.p3: What actually comes off a DevEx payout

notCovered.regionalPricing: Regional pricing adjustments, which change what a player pays without changing your share percentage.
notCovered.resale: Limited or resale items, where the resale fee structure differs from a first sale.
notCovered.groupSplits: Group revenue splits agreed between collaborators, which happen after Roblox's commission.
notCovered.promotional: Any promotional or programme-specific rate Roblox may apply to a particular category.
notCovered.devexConversion: The DevEx conversion, which is a separate step handled by the main calculator.

prose.priceFloors: Price floors differ by item category and Roblox has adjusted them over time, so hardcoding one universal floor would produce wrong answers for most items. Entering the multiple keeps the result correct whatever your category’s floor happens to be.

conversions.intro: A server-rendered table of common amounts across all three documented rates, plus an input for anything not listed.
conversions.convertAnyDescription: Not every amount needs its own page. Enter yours here and share the resulting link.
conversions.everyAmountDescription: Sixty-eight amounts at all three documented rates, including the ones below the DevEx minimum — those are asked about most often, and the honest answer includes the fact that they cannot be cashed out. Every figure is rendered on the server, so it is here whether or not JavaScript runs.
conversions.fullBreakdownDescription: These amounts have enough demand and enough to say about them to justify a page of their own. The rest are served by the table above and by the calculator.
conversions.roundingDescription: Displayed to the cent, calculated with more precision than that.

detailed.p1: This list is deliberately short. A page for every number would be a page that says nothing new, which is both unhelpful and against search-quality guidance. Amounts are added only when they clear a demand threshold and there is something specific to say about them.

rounding.p1: Each figure is Robux multiplied by an exact decimal rate, held as a fraction throughout and rounded to the cent only when it is printed. Nothing is rounded partway through, so a total never disagrees with the sum of its parts.

prose.notRoundNumbers: The list is not a selection of round numbers: it is the amounts that are actually searched for. Anything not here — including figures larger than the table’s last row — goes into the converter above, which uses the same rates and the same arithmetic.

amountPage.headlineDescription: At the current standard rate, before any payment-provider fee or tax.
amountPage.allThreeDescription: Roblox decides which rate applies to which part of a balance. This shows what each would pay.
amountPage.reachingDescription: Working the other way: what payout targets this balance covers.
amountPage.reachingLabel: Payout targets and whether this amount covers them
amountPage.nearbyDescription: Adjacent amounts with their own detailed breakdown.

context.robux30000: 30,000 is the amount that matters most, because it is the minimum Earned Robux balance Roblox requires before a DevEx request can be submitted at all. Below this figure the question is not what the payout would be but whether a request can be made.
context.robux50000: 50,000 Earned Robux clears the minimum with room to spare, so it is a common first cash-out for a creator whose experience has just started earning consistently.
context.robux100000: 100,000 is the most searched round figure in this range, and it is the point where the gap between the current and legacy rates becomes large enough to notice: thirty dollars separates them.
context.robux200000: At 200,000 Earned Robux a creator is usually cashing out on a schedule rather than as a one-off, which makes the difference between rate buckets worth tracking rather than estimating.
context.robux300000: 300,000 Earned Robux is ten times the DevEx minimum. It is a useful reference point for a creator working out how many cash-out cycles a year of earnings represents.
context.robux500000: Half a million Earned Robux is the scale at which payment-provider fees and personal tax obligations stop being rounding errors, which is why this page links directly to the fees and taxes guide.
context.robux1000000: A million Robux is the headline milestone creators actually search for, and it is the clearest illustration of why purchase price and DevEx payout are not the same number.
context.robux10000000: Ten million Earned Robux represents sustained earnings from a large experience. At this scale the split between standard and legacy balances, and any qualifying U.S. 18+ portion, changes the total by thousands of dollars.

amountPage.clearsMinimum: That is {multiple} times the {minimum} Earned Robux minimum, so it clears the threshold to submit a request. Clearing the threshold is not approval — Roblox reviews every request.
amountPage.belowMinimum: This is below the {minimum} Earned Robux minimum, so a DevEx request cannot be submitted at this balance yet.
